Talent
TAL-ent
n.
Hebrew kikkār (a round, a circuit; hence a round weight); Greek talanton, “a balance, weight, sum of money.” The largest unit of weight in the ancient world; estimates vary but a talent was approximately 75 lb (34 kg) of silver, equivalent to many years’ wages for a laborer.

Biblical Definition

The talent was the largest unit of weight and currency in the ancient biblical world—a sum so substantial that it functioned as the standard for major financial transactions, royal tributes, and the metal weights used in the construction of the tabernacle and temple. A single talent of silver was approximately 75 lb (34 kg), worth many years’ wages for an ordinary laborer; a talent of gold was correspondingly more valuable. The construction of the tabernacle used twenty and nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels of gold and an hundred talents, and a thousand seven hundred and threescore and fifteen shekels of silver (Ex 38:24-25)—a substantial concentration of precious metals dedicated to the sanctuary. Solomon’s temple construction involved still vaster sums: 100,000 talents of gold and a million talents of silver among the materials David prepared (1 Chr 22:14). The Queen of Sheba brought 120 talents of gold as a gift to Solomon (1 Kgs 10:10). Naaman offered Elisha 10 talents of silver and 6,000 pieces of gold for his cleansing (which Elisha refused; 2 Kgs 5:5). The most famous biblical use of the talent, however, is figurative: Christ’s parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30. A man traveling into a far country delivers to his servants his goods: and unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey. The two who put their talents to work doubling them are commended at the master’s return; the one who buried his talent in the earth is rebuked and his talent given to the one with ten. The parable’s lesson is structural to Christian discipleship. The Lord has entrusted to every servant some measure of His gifts (the same word talent has in English come to mean natural gift or aptitude precisely through this parable’s influence); each is to put those gifts to work for the Master’s purposes; faithful stewardship is rewarded and unfaithful neglect is judged; the disparity of original distribution (five, two, one) does not change the principle (each is responsible for the use of what he received). The talent therefore has both a literal-biblical-economic dimension (the largest unit of ancient weight and currency, used for major royal and sacred transactions) and a derived-figurative dimension (the entrusted gifts of the Master, for which every servant gives account at the day of reckoning).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TALENT as among the ancients, a weight, and a coin; the value of which varied; in the New Testament, a sum of about 750 ounces of silver or its equivalent; figuratively, intellectual ability, natural gift, or any endowment whether moral or physical, considered as gifts from God for which we are accountable.

expand to see more

TALENT, n. — 1. Among the ancients, a weight, and a coin. The Attic talent of silver was 60 minae, or 6,000 drachms. 2. Figuratively, faculty; natural gift or endowment; a metaphorical application of the word, supposed to be borrowed from the parable in the gospel, Matt 25. Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury? (Luke 19:23).

TALENTED, a. — Furnished with talents.

Key Scripture

Matthew 25:14-15 — "For the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods. And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey."

Matthew 25:21 — "His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord."

1 Chronicles 22:14 — "Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the house of the LORD an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight; for it is in abundance."

Matthew 18:24 — "And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents."

Modern Corruption

The talent doctrine is corrupted by the secularized derivation that has retained the figurative sense (natural gift or aptitude) while losing the parable’s underlying claim that the gifts are entrusted by the Master and that every servant must give account at His return—and by the inverse error of the burying-the-talent pattern that the parable explicitly judges.

expand to see more

The word talent in modern English means natural gift or aptitude—a usage derived directly from Christ’s parable but secularized in the process. Where the parable explicitly grounds the gifts in the Master who entrusted them and the day of reckoning when account must be given, modern usage retains the gift-sense and drops the stewardship-frame: his talents are now spoken of as his own, the products of his nature or upbringing, with no reference to the Giver or to any future accounting. The Christian recovery is the parable’s own framing. The talents are entrusted by the Lord; the servant is steward, not owner; the gifts are given according to his several ability—the Master’s sovereign distribution apportioning differently to different servants; the responsibility is in proportion to what was received; the day of reckoning is coming when each servant will give account of his stewardship. The Christian therefore relates to his abilities, opportunities, time, money, education, and gifts as a steward returning the Master’s deposit with increase—not as an autonomous owner accountable to no one.

The opposite corruption is the buried-talent pattern that the parable explicitly judges. The one-talent servant’s reasoning is a model of how the unfaithful steward justifies his unfruitfulness: I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine. The Master’s response is severe: thou wicked and slothful servant... thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents. The lesson is sober. Unfaithful stewardship—the burying of the gift, the failure to put it to work, the rationalization that the Master is too hard to risk loss—is not innocent neglect but actively judged. The contemporary believer who has buried his ministerial gift, his teaching gift, his financial means, his time, his opportunity, his platform, in the soft earth of safety and convenience is the one-talent servant of the parable, and the Master’s reckoning at His return is the same. Recover both ends. Refuse the secularized derivation that severs the gifts from the Giver, and refuse the burying-the-talent pattern that wastes the deposit. The faithful steward puts the talents to work, multiplies them for the Master’s purposes, and at the day of reckoning hears well done, thou good and faithful servant... enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kikkār (a round weight) and Greek talanton (balance, weight, large sum of money); the largest unit of ancient weight and currency, used for tabernacle and temple construction, royal tributes, and (figuratively, through Christ’s parable) the entrusted gifts of the Master for which every servant gives account.

expand to see more

Hebrew kikkār (H3603) — round weight, talent (the OT word).

Greek talanton (G5007) — talent (Matt 18:24; 25:14-30).

Greek didomi + talanton — idiomatic for entrusting (Matt 25:15, “he gave talents”).

Modern English talent — natural gift or aptitude (the secularized derivation from Christ’s parable).

Usage

"To every man according to his several ability—the Master’s sovereign distribution apportioning differently to different servants."

"The buried-talent pattern of the parable is the contemporary believer’s standing temptation: rationalized neglect of the Master’s deposit on grounds of safety and convenience."

"Modern talent retains the gift-sense and drops the stewardship-frame; Christian recovery is the parable’s own framing: gifts entrusted, account to be given, faithfulness rewarded and slothful neglect judged."
